headline: Bunker pinned tight on the south beaches, blues working them from Second to Weekapaug
subhead: Bass have gone to bed until dark, tog are still a scattered pre-season story, but the bluefish blitz is the realest thing happening on the rocks right now.
body_markdown:
Bunker are stacked so thick against the sand at Second Beach this week you can see the school turn dark, then silver, then dark again as it rolls with the swell. That's the tell. When the bait balls up tight like that and won't leave the wash, something's pushing it, and this week it's blues — not albies, not yet — but a real, sustained bluefish blitz working the south-facing beaches from Second all the way down through Charlestown Breachway and out toward Weekapaug. We flagged this exact pattern building last week, said it'd keep spreading as long as the bunker stayed pinned and the weather stayed calm, and that's exactly what's playing out. Calm mornings, light southwest air in the afternoons, water sitting warm on the surface — the bait has nowhere to go and the blues know it.

I've been working these blitzes with a simple approach: park the truck where I can see the bait nervous, walk down, and throw a Hopkins or a Kastmaster in silver/blue right into the froth. No finesse needed. Blues this size — mostly 3 to 6 pounds with the occasional bigger fish mixed in — will hit anything that moves fast through the melee. Tin lures, poppers, even a bare bucktail dragged through it. The trick out here on the rocky stretches is footing, not presentation. Charlestown Breachway's rock jetty has been a good stage for this — bait gets funneled through the cut on the outgoing and the blues pile up right where the current speeds up against the rocks. Fish the last two hours of the ebb there and you'll find them.

Striped bass are the quieter half of this story right now, and if you're expecting daytime bass action on the south shore, you're going to be disappointed. Surface temps have pushed well into the 70s along here, same story as the rest of southern New England, and the bass have done what they do this time of year — they've gone deep and nocturnal. I'm not seeing much daytime bass activity on the ledges at all, even around usually reliable structure like the rocks off Sakonnet Point or the drop-offs at Napatree. If you want stripers this week, you're fishing dusk into full dark. Eels and bunker chunks fished on the bottom around the deeper ledges off Brenton Point or the rock piles at the mouth of the Sakonnet River have been the play after 9pm. Don't waste daylight hours on bass right now — put that time into the bluefish or scout for albies instead.

Speaking of albies — nothing confirmed yet in our waters, but I'd be watching close over the next week to ten days. Water's climbing into the range where the first push usually shows, and Block Island sits close enough that fish moving into that corridor tend to filter into Sakonnet Point and eventually Napatree not long after. I haven't heard a single confirmed hookup yet on this stretch, so don't let anyone tell you different — but the conditions are lining up the way they usually do right before the first fish show. I'll be walking the rocks at Sakonnet Point with a bag of small Deadly Dicks and Albie Snax just in case, because when they do show, it's usually with zero warning.

Tog fishing right now is early and patchy — this isn't peak season yet, but a few guys have been picking at fish on green crabs around the deeper humps off Jamestown and the rockpiles outside Newport Harbor on the slack tide. Nothing worth planning a trip around specifically, but if you're already out there working blues and want to drop a bait, it's not a bad time to start scouting which cracks are holding fish for when the real bite kicks in come September and October. I like fishing green crab on a simple high-low rig, small hooks, right on the edge where the rock face drops into deeper water — 15 to 25 feet on the outside ledges. Patience pays more than volume at this point in the season.

Fluke have been a mixed bag off the south shore — plenty of shorts working the sandy stretches inside Charlestown Pond and around the Harbor of Refuge, but keeper-class fish are harder to come by unless you're working deeper water. The channel edges outside Point Judith and the deeper humps off Watch Hill Reef have given up some better fish — 20 to 22 inches — on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, fished slow on the drift in 25 to 35 feet. Stronger tide stages have produced better than the slack, which tracks — moving water keeps the bigger fish active instead of buried in the mud.

Looking ahead, I'd keep my time split between the bluefish blitz during daylight and bass after dark, because right now those are the two honest programs on this stretch. If the bunker schools hold along the beachfront through the week — and there's no sign yet of them breaking up — expect the blue bite to keep spreading further along the coast, same as it has been. The bigger story to watch is the albies. Conditions are lining up. I wouldn't book a charter around it yet, but I'd have the light tackle rigged and ready, because when that first fish shows at Sakonnet or Napatree, it won't give you much notice.
